name: Kibosy Kiantalaotsy-Majunga
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: There are two dialects with limited intercomprehensability: Kisakalava, used in a dozen villages with some twenty thousand speakers, and Kiantalautsi, spoken mostly in two villages, Ouangani and Poroani, by a few thousand speakers [1]. ... Second, general observations of Kibushi suggest that there may be differences in word stress across villages and dialects. ... Stress in both Kibushi dialects is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [͡tra] and [na] [7]. ... the median duration of stressed syllables is ... 287 ms for Ouangani (vs. 190 ms) and 270 ms for Poroani (vs. 179 ms).
new_statements.citation: Kassime, Ahamada, Fabrice Hirsch & Miki Mori. 2023. Vowel space and acoustic characteristics of stressed syllables in two kibushi dialects spoken in Mayotte, France: a pilot study. Proceedings of the 20th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2023), Prague, pp. 3321-3324. HAL hal-04198178.
new_statements.locator: Section 1 Introduction, p. 3321 (PDF p. 2, right column); dialect identification in Abstract p. 3321; duration results sec. 3.2.1, pp. 3322-3323
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in both Kibushi dialects of Mayotte, including Kiantalautsi (Ouangani, Poroani); it may instead fall on the antepenult when the word ends in one of the weak syllables ka, tra, na (the pan-Malagasy pattern). The authors' own measurements on Kiantalautsi speakers show the (penult) stressed syllable is markedly longer, with an F0 rise and an intensity peak.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress 'can also' occur in words ending in [ka], [tra], [na] (stated with a citation to a Malagasy intonation study; whether all such words or a lexical subset is not said). Test words like ꞌlela(ka), ꞌholu(ŋu), ꞌvoru(ŋu) are transcribed with stress staying on the root penult when the optional final syllable is present.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word stress ('differences in word stress across villages and dialects'); data are isolated Swadesh-list words (citation forms). The 2024 poster adds that in read declarative sentences stressed syllables remain longer and high pitch sits mostly on penultimate/ultimate syllables of the predicate.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog bush1250 'Kibosy Kiantalaotsy-Majunga' is the Kiantalautsi (Antalaotsy) variety of Malagasy spoken in Mayotte (villages Ouangani, Poroani; historically linked to the Antalaotsy of Mahajanga/Majunga), placed directly under North-Central Malagasic. The quoted source (Kassime, Hirsch & Mori 2023) studies BOTH Kibushi dialects of Mayotte and states the rule for 'both Kibushi dialects': Kiantalautsi (= bush1250; speakers recorded in Ouangani and Poroani) and Kisakalava (= Kibushi-Kimaore, kibu1236, a dialect of Antankarana Malagasy anta1255). The same paper is already the catalog source for anta1255; for bush1250 it is on-languoid because Kiantalautsi speakers were measured and named. Nothing reached describes the Madagascar-side Antalaotsy of Majunga.

sources.locator: Section 1 Introduction, p. 3321 (PDF p. 2, right column); dialect identification in Abstract p. 3321; duration results sec. 3.2.1, pp. 3322-3323
sources.note: p.3321: 'Stress in both Kibushi dialects [Kisakalava and Kiantalautsi] is penultimate, just as in the Malagasy language (Merina dialect). But it can also fall on the antepenultimate syllable with words that end in [ka], [tra] and [na]'; measures duration/F0/intensity of penult-stressed syllables in 19 words from 9 Kiantalautsi (Ouangani, Poroani) and 19 Kisakalava speakers; stressed syllables systematically longer (Ouangani 287 vs 190 ms, Poroani 270 vs 179 ms).

sources.citation: Kassime, Ahamada, Fabrice Hirsch & Miki Mori. 2024. Prosodic variation of Kibushi dialects (Mayotte, France) via the reading of The Little Prince: a pilot study. Poster, 13th International Seminar on Speech Production, Autrans. HAL hal-04583373.
sources.note: Sentence-level prosody in read speech (Acoua, Chiconi = Kisakalava; Ouangani = Kiantalautsi): 'Stressed syllables exhibit longer durations than unstressed ones across all three villages'; high pitch in declaratives mostly on penultimate and ultimate syllables of the predicate; no restatement of the word-stress rule.
